WAKE
he China Clipper continued
across the Pacific stepping
stones to Midway and Wake
Islands. The flight from
Honolulu to Midway took 8
hours, 56 minutes. The leg from
Midway to Wake was another 8 hours.
23 minutes. At the time, both Midway
and Wake were barren atolls. Captain
Musick described the flight to Wake. It
was "the shortest but most difficult
span in the entire aerial bridge and
called for one of the most exacting
feats of navigation on record - striking
on the nose of a tiny point smaller than
a pinhead on the vast map of the
Pacific Ocean."
The China Clipper brought the
Pan Am base staffs 12 crates of turkeys,
cartons of cranberries, sweet potatoes
and mince meat for the first Thanks-
giving dinners in the history of these
islands. The China Clipper also carried
25 canaries requested by the airport
manager "to enliven the deadly silence
of isolated Wake Island." The China
Clipper Il is carrying a similar cargo of
Thanksgiving turkeys to the military
bases at Midway and Wake. But thanks
to television and the other noises of the
modern world, canaries were no longer
deemed necessary on Wake Island.

Welcome aboard the China Clipper II. Fifty years ago today, the China
Clipper, a Pan Am Martin M-130 flying boat, taxied out into the harbor of
San Francisco Bay and took off trailing a large wake of sea sprav. Bands
played and flags waved. Cheering crowds lined the shores. A flotilla of
pleasure boats dotted the harbor and small planes flew overhead to
witness the historic event the inauguration of the first commercial
transpacific airmail service from San Francisco to Manila by the China
Clipper. Recognizing the significance of the moment, President Franklin
D. Roosevelt sent a special message "conveying heartfelt congratulations
of an airminded sailor."
Today, we commemorate this historic flight by retracing the route of the
China Clipper aboard a Boeing 747 Jet Clipper. The flight of the China
Clipper Il not only celebrates past achievements, but serves as a reminder
of the advances made in aviation. We pay tribute to the individual and
collective efforts of the men and women who pioneered Pan Am's air
routes across the Pacific. We are honored that you are joining Pan Am on
this nostalgic flight into history in salute to the China Clipper.
PACIFIC OCEAN
SAN FRANCISCO
MIDWAY
MANILA
C. Shine Cak
C. Edward Acker
Chairman
n November 22, 1935 at 3:46 pm (local time), the China
Clipper took off from the Pan American operating base at
Alameda, California enroute to Manila. The route had
previously been charted by survey missions flown by Pan
Am. The 8,210-mile journey included stops in Honolulu,
Midway, Wake and Guam Islands, arriving in Manila exactly on schedule
on November 29. Total elapsed time was 6 days, 7 hours and 46 minutes.
Total flying time was 59 hours, 48 minutes.
The China Clipper had a crew of seven with Pan Am's veteran chief
pilot Captain Edwin C. Musick in command. This first transpacific airmail
flight carried 58 bags of mail with 110,865 letters bound for Honolulu.
Guam and Manila. Today, the China Clipper Il is carrying approximately
180,000 letters.

HONOLULU
he China Clipper traveled
the 2,400-mile leg from San
Francisco to Honolulu in
21 hours, 5 minutes. Today,
this flight will take approxi-
mately 5 hours, 15 minutes. In his
radio dispatch from the flight deck,
Captain Musick described the journey:
"Twelve hundred miles out over
the Pacific and drilling through the
black void of the night, the China
Clipper is in close contact with all
points of the compass after eight hours
of steady flying through layers of clouds
above and below...As night is thinning
into the grayness of dawn, all is quiet.
From 10,000 feet above, the sea in the
gray light is glassy, with long unbroken
swells. A flood of color suddenly
spreads across that surface. Night
has gone.
On its arrival in Hawaii on November
23, Captain Musick said. "The enthu-
siastic welcome of the crowds in
Honolulu seems to merge with the
similarly expressed honors in San
Francisco which are still humming in
our ears"

GUAM
nroute to Guam, Captain Musick radioed from the flight deck,
"Everthing was functioning perfectly and the China Clipper
settled down to the long 1,500-mile drive ahead. The cloud
moisture on the wings flashed every color of the spectrum and
the propellers described great glistening arcs as we sped ahead
in a world all to ourselves -except for the nine radio stations and the three
radio compass stations that kept their invisible fingers on us.
The China Clipper crossed the International Date Line and arrived in
Guam 45 minutes ahead of schedule. After a day of rest and Thanksgiving
dinner at the Governor's Palace, the crew of the China Clipper was ready
to embark on the final leg of their journey.

MANILA
he 1,600-mile leg from
Guam to Manila was the
only stretch that had never
before been flown on survey
missions by Pan Am. In his
dispatch from Manila, Captain Musick
said: "As the rugged hills of the Philip-
pines appeared over the port bow
today, the crew of the China Clipper
came to a realization of the significance
of this achievement for American
aviation -
-a history-making 8,000-mile
flight in a four-motored transport plane
bearing the first transpacific mail from
Alameda, California to Manila."
Arriving in Manila right on schedule
at 3:32 pm local time on November
29, the China Clipper was greeted by
exuberant crowds. Asked by curious
reporters to describe their journey.
Captain Musick simply stated: "The
flight was without incident."
